title: Letting go of roles
tomorrow: Baba asks for his phone. who hasn't he called in years?

lines: YOUR TURN TO READ IT TO ME.
cards: Hand-me-downs carry a smell: a jacket that smells like a cousin's closet, a recipe card spotted with oil. Baba Kartar's bundle smells of cardamom and an old cupboard.
He holds it out in both hands: a faded cloth, tied at the corners. Inside is his gutka, the small book of daily prayers. The corners are soft as felt.
The spine has a crack where it has opened at the same place for longer than Simran has been alive. Your turn to read it to me, he says. My eyes are done with small print.
She doesn't take it right away.

teach.b: Sikhs have a story about handing on that is all objects and hands. When Guru Nanak chose who would carry the light after him, he didn't choose by blood.
Satta and Balvand, minstrels whose ballad is in the Guru Granth Sahib, sing it on Ang 966 and 967: in paraphrase, Nanak set the canopy over Lehna's head, and his sons did not keep faith.
Tradition adds the things you could touch: a coconut and coins set down before Lehna, and Guru Nanak, the teacher, bowing to his student.
Lehna was given a new name, Angad, which tradition links to ang, a limb: part of my own body.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO HANDS IT ON BOWS.
teach.b: Here's the line for a friend tonight: in the Sikh story, the Guru who hands it on bows first. Letting go of a role isn't shrinking.

teach.h: ANGAD: A LIMB OF MY OWN.
teach.b: The giver is still the giver; the light didn't leave Nanak, it went on through Angad. Simran takes the gutka.
The cloth is warm from Baba's lap. She opens it at the crack, and it falls open by itself.

how: Some Sikh families pass a gutka, a kara or a family Granth from one generation to the next, wrapped in a cloth; Sikhs remember Guru Nanak installing Guru Angad as the model of handing on.

games.q: what does “letting go of roles” mean?
o: changing who you are to fit a new place
handing a duty on to the next person, with grace
quitting a job you no longer want to do

games.q: what was handed on — tap the pairs.
p: the student Nanak chose, not by blood
a new name, linked to ang, a limb

s: Guru Nanak passed the Guruship to his own son
Satta and Balvand, Ang 967: his sons did not keep faith; he chose Lehna.
in the story, the Guru bows to his successor
tradition says Guru Nanak set offerings before Lehna and bowed to him.
handing on a role means you matter less
the light didn't leave Nanak; it went on through Angad.

games.q: you started a club at school; you're graduating. the new leader wants to change the name. what does today's story suggest?
o: hand it on fully, cheer them on, and let them make it theirs.
stay on as adviser and keep final say, just in case.
hand it on, but only after they agree to keep everything the same.
games.why: Guru Nanak set the canopy over Lehna and bowed to him. handing on, done with grace, means the next one carries it.

practice: Find one object near you that someone handed on to you, or one you might hand on someday: a book, a ring, a mug, a tool. Hold it in both hands. Feel its weight, smell it, find the place where it's worn.
Let the sit be just you and the thing.

wordCard.voice: Letting go of roles. In the Sikh story, Guru Nanak hands the light to Angad and bows to him: handing on is a gift, not a loss.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Angad, the name given to Bhai Lehna; tradition links it to ang, a limb.

carryVoice: Pocket this: pass it on, and bow while you do it, the way Nanak did. Hands open, day done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 966-967 (Ramkali ki Vaar, Satta and Balvand: the canopy over Lehna; the sons who did not keep faith), paraphrased
Guru Nanak installing Bhai Lehna as Guru Angad (janamsakhi tradition: coconut and coins, the bow)
